MiR-145 encapsulated small extracellular 
vesicles inhibit colorectal cancer progression 
by downregulating fascin actin-bundling 
protein 1 expression

Yanxia Chen1,2,6, Meijuan He3, Lei Cui4, Jianguo Zhang1, Hanpeng Huang3* and Zhimin Tao1,2,5*

Abstract
Background  Drug degradation poses a significant challenge in the pursuit of effective gene therapies for cancers.

Methods  Here we have developed a bioactive nanosized composite that utilizes human umbilical cord 
mesenchymal stem cells (hucMSCs) derived small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), to carry tumor suppressor miR-145 
alongside erbium-doped rare earth nanoparticles (ErNPs). This approach not only enhances in vivo delivery but 
also facilitates real-time fluorescence tracking of nucleic acid drugs in the near infrared (NIR) II window. With this 
technique, we are able to realize and visualize the effective inhibition of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression in a 
xenografted murine model.

Results  Our results revealed that the efficient loading of miR-145 into sEVs could be achieved through a dynamic 
combination of sonication and electroporation. The resulting miR-145-encapsulated sEVs (i.e., miRNA@sEVs) exhibited 
a profound ability to hinder tumor growth by effectively downregulating the expression of fascin actin-bundling 
protein 1 (FSCN1), both in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, the circulation half-time of miRNA@sEVs was measured to 
be ~ 4 h and the fluorescence at the tumor sites reached a peak intensity at ~ 8 h after intravenous injection of sEVs 
particles. Finally, the fluorescent signals of miRNA@sEVs were predominantly localized in the mouse liver and spleen, 
with substantial accumulation in tumors.

Conclusions  Our results illuminated the excellent biosafety of miRNA@sEVs and their high accumulation in tumors, 
leading to efficient suppression of tumor progression. This research heralds a promising advancement in gene 
therapy, paving the way for more effective and safer treatment options.

Introduction
Colorectal  cancer  (CRC)  is  one  of  the  most  prevalent 
malignancies  worldwide.  While  its  incidence  typically 
rises  with  age,  an  alarming  trend  shows  that  younger 
adults  are  increasingly  at  risk  as  well  [1].  In  the  United 
States,  CRC  tragically  remains  the  second  leading  cause 
of  cancer-related  deaths,  with  153,020  new  cases  diag-
nosed  and  52,550  death  tolls  in  2023  [2].  The  carcino-
genesis of CRC is characterized by a series of progressive 
genetic  changes  through  multiple  pathways,  leading  to 
tumor  formation,  growth,  migration  and  local  or  dis-
tant metastasis, often resulting in diagnoses at advanced 
stages  when  treatment  options  become  very  limited  [3, 
4].  Conventional  treatments  for  CRC  include  surgery, 
chemotherapy,  and  immunotherapy,  playing  essential 
roles in combating this disease. In addition, gene therapy 
is  emerging  as  an  innovative  alternative.  Targeting  the 
frequently  altered  TP53  and  KRAS,  this  cutting-edge 
approach offers hope for many facing CRC [5]. This gene 
intervention  holds  promise  as  a  safe  and  reliable  treat-
ment  strategy  with  reduced  side  effects,  lighting  a  path 
forward  in  the  quest  for  effective  cancer  treatments  in 
clinical settings [6].

MicroRNA (miRNA) as a non-coding small RNA mol-
ecule  that  regulates  gene  expression,  can  interfere  with 
specific oncogenic pathways [7]. Among the most studied 
miRNAs in CRC, miR-145 has been identified as a potent 
suppressor  of  tumorigenesis,  progression,  and  metasta-
sis, which intricately engages with various tumor-specific 
pathways,  including  KRAS  and  P53  signaling  [8].  The 
expression  level  of  miR-145  was  found  significantly  cor-
related with poor prognosis of patients with a diversity of 
malignant tumors, including colorectal, gastric, and ovar-
ian cancers [9, 10]. Simultaneously, the level of miR-145 
in the blood plasma predicted the CRC risk in the general 
population, making it a practical biomarker in early diag-
nosis of CRC [11]. However, the gene targets of miR-145 
can  be  multiple,  as  the  primary  target  in  CRC  progres-
sion remains elusive, which may otherwise enrich thera-
peutic regimen greatly.

As  many  gene  therapy  techniques  require  viral  vec-
tors  (e.g.,  adeno-associated  virus)  to  carry  therapeutic 
nucleic  acids,  it  raises  concerns  of  immunogenicity  and 
cytotoxicity  in  clinical  contexts.  Alternatively,  non-viral 
formulations,  primarily  composed  of  lipids  and  poly-
mers,  have  emerged  as  safe  and  effective  vehicles  for 
delivering  genetic  substances.  Among  those  biocompat-
ible  materials,  extracellular  vesicles  (EVs)  are  a  group  of 
membraned  particles  secreted  by  most  types  of  living 
cells.  They  exhibit  a  range  of  physicochemical  proper-
ties,  such  as  different  sizes  and  densities,  and  biological 
characteristics  related  to  their  diverse  origins  and  the 
resulting surface and interior compositions [12]. EVs can 
be categorized into small EVs (sEVs), measuring less than 

200  nm  in  diameter,  and  medium/large  EVs  that  exceed 
this size [13]. Often referred to as exosomes, sEVs possess 
a typical ‘cup-shaped’ structure and exist in most biologi-
cal  fluids,  including  saliva,  blood,  and  urine  [14].  Their 
surfaces are enriched with transmembrane proteins that 
are capable of relocation within the cellular matrix, facili-
tating  the  exchange  of  materials  and  signaling  between 
cells  [15].  Compared  to  artificially  synthesized  particles 
of  similar  size,  sEVs  own  naturally  derived  membrane 
structures  of  lipid  bilayer,  so  offering  many  unmatched 
features  as  a  delivery  platform,  including  low  immuno-
genicity,  non-toxicity,  exceptional  biocompatibility  and 
stability [16].

In this study, we utilized sEVs derived from hucMSCs 
as  gene  carriers.  Those  sEVs  were  loaded  with  miR-145 
and ErNPs for in vivo miRNA delivery and fluorescence 
tracking. The employment of ErNPs as an NIR II emissive 
fluorescent  probe  provided  an  unprecedented  imaging 
window  for  biological  tissues  [17].  Compared  to  tradi-
tional NIR I dyes, which have an emission wavelength of 
650–900 nm, ErNPs emit a peak wavelength at 1540 nm. 
This  allows  deeper  tissue  penetration  with  minimized 
spontaneous  fluorescence,  so  enabling  precise  localiza-
tion  of  the  transported  particles  in  murine  CRC  mod-
els.  Concurrently,  this  study  validated  the  interaction 
between  the  tumor  suppressor  miR-145  and  its  cancer-
ous  targets  in  CRC,  shedding  light  on  the  anti-cancer 
mechanisms of gene therapies.

Materials and methods
Human CRC tissue samples

Sixty-two  CRC  samples  (24  rectum  and  38  colon  tis-
sues)  were  clinically  diagnosed  and  histopathologically 
confirmed at theAffiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University 
(AHJU)  between  March  2023  and  February  2024,  and 
preserved  at  -80  °C,  together  with  their  corresponding 
paracancerous  tissues.  All  cancerous  tissues  were  his-
tologically  adenocarcinomas  surgically  removed  from 
patients  that  received  no  prior  treatment.  Patient  infor-
mation  was  summarized  in  Table  S1.  Informed  consent 
was  acquired  from  patients  and  ethical  approval  was 
obtained from the research ethics committees of AHJU.

Isolation, characterization and culture of hucMSCs

HucMSCs  were  isolated  as  previously  reported  [18,  19]. 
In  brief,  following  approval  from  the  Research  Ethics 
Committee  of  AHJU  and  with  informed  consent  from 
patients,  fresh  umbilical  cord  tissues  were  obtained. 
HucMSCs  were  isolated  using  the  tissue  block  adhe-
sion  method  and  cultured  in  an  alpha  minimum  essen-
tial  medium  (α-MEM,  Invitrogen,  USA)  with  10%  fetal 
bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA). The isolated hucMSCs 
were characterized as reported [20].

HucMSCs  were  transferred  to  a  10  cm  culture  dish 
with  the  number  of  1 × 106  cells.  When  the  cell  density 
reached  50–70%  confluence  in  1–2  days,  the  medium 
was  replaced  with  α-MEM  containing  10%  EV-depleted 
FBS for 8 mL/dish. Then the cells were cultured at 37 °C 
in the incubator with 5% CO2 for 48 h. Next, the super-
natant  from  the  cell  culture  of  hucMSCs  was  collected 
and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 20 min at 4 °C to remove 
cell  debris.  Subsequently,  centrifugation  was  continued 
at  10,000  g  for  30  min  at  4  °C  to  eliminate  cell  organ-
elles.  The  supernatant  was  then  transferred  to  100  kDa 
molecular  weight  cut-off  (MWCO)  ultrafiltration  tubes 
(Millipore, USA) and centrifuged at 1,500 g for 30 min at 
4 °C for multiple times until the concentration of vesicles 
reached  100×  of  original  solutions,  i.e.,  the  volume  of 
the  concentrated  solution  is  1/100  of  the  initial  amount 
when cell supernatant was first collected. Next, the con-
centrated solution was transferred to high-speed centri-
fuge  tubes  and  centrifuged  at  4  °C,  100,000  g  for  1.5  h 
(Beckman, USA). Then the supernatant was carefully dis-
carded, and fresh PBS was added to the tubes to wash the 
precipitate, followed by centrifugation again at 4 °C and 
100,000  g  for  1.5  h.  After  centrifugation,  the  hucMSC-
derived sEVs were obtained as precipitates. To character-

Western blot

Total  proteins  in  cells,  sEVs  and  tissues  were  extracted 
using radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) lysis buffer 
containing protease inhibitors. Proteins of equal quantity 
in each group were separated by sodium dodecyl sulfate-
polyacrylamide  gel  electrophoresis  (SDS-PAGE),  fol-
lowed by transfer of the gel onto a polyvinylidene fluoride 
(PVDF)  membrane.  After  the  transfer,  the  membrane 
was blocked with 5% skim milk for 2 h. Subsequently, the 
PVDF membrane was incubated overnight with primary 
antibodies  specific  to  each  protein  at  4  °C,  including 
anti-Alix,  anti-TSG101,  anti-CD9,  anti-Calnexin  (1:500, 
Cell  Signaling  Technology,  USA),  anti-FSCN1  (1:1000, 
Abcam,  USA),  and  anti-GAPDH  (1:3000,  Abcam,  USA). 
Later, the PVDF membrane was incubated with a horse-
radish  peroxidase  (HRP)-labeled  secondary  antibody 
(1:2000) (Vazyme, China). After washing, the membrane 
was detected by chemiluminescence imaging instrument 
(GE, USA).

qRT-PCR analysis

Trizol  lysis  buffer  was  employed  to  extract  mRNA  from 
cells  and  tissues.  The  exosomal  RNA  purification  kit 
(Qiagen,  Germany)  was  utilized  to  isolate  miRNA  from 
sEVs,  and  the  reverse  transcription  kit  (Vazyme,  China) 
was used for reverse transcription of miRNA and mRNA. 
Subsequently, QuantStudio 3 was employed for qRT-PCR 
analysis.  The  primer  sequences  used  in  the  experiment 
were shown in Table 1.

Transfection of miRNA and plasmids

All  the  miRNA  mimics,  miRNA  inhibitors  and  negtive 
control (NC) used in the experiment were obtained from 
Genepharma  Co.,  Ltd.,  China.  The  synthetic  miRNA 
comprised of 21-base pair nucleotides. NC has a scram-
bled  sequence  of  nucleotides  that  undergoe  random 
rearrangement (i.e., in a shuffling order) while maintain-
ing  the  same  length  and  GC  content  as  the  miR-145. 
Cells  were  seeded  in  6-well  plates  (2 × 105  cells/well). 
When the cell density reached 60–70%, cells were trans-
fected  with  miRNA  and  plasmid  using  Lipofectamine 
2000  (Invitrogen,  USA)  in  serum-free  medium  accord-
ing  to  the  manufacturer’s  instructions.  Firstly,  the  origi-
nal  culture  medium  was  gently  discarded  and  the  cells 
were  washed  twice  with  fresh  PBS. Then  0.5  mL  of  cul-
ture  medium  without  FBS  was  added,  and  the  cell  plate 
was cultured in the cell incubator for 1–2 h. During the 
incubation,  the  transfection  reagent  was  prepared,  as  5

µL  of  Lipofectamine  2000  (Invitrogen,  USA)  was  added 
to 245 µL Opti MEM medium, with gently mixing, then

tions were transferred to the same tube and mixed gently, 
left  at  room  temperature  for  20  min.  Then,  500  µL  of 
mixed solution was added to each well and the plate was 
cultured in the cell incubator for 6–8 h. Next, the culture 
medium  containing  transfection  reagent  was  carefully 
discarded  and  replaced  with  the  fresh  medium  contain-
ing 10% FBS, and the plate was cultured in the incubator 
for 24–48 h.

Dual-luciferase reporter gene analysis

Human  CRC  cell  lines  HCT116  and  SW480  were  pur-
chased  from  Institute  of  Biochemistry  and  Cell  Biol-
ogy  at  the  Chinese  Academy  of  Sciences  (Shanghai, 
China)  and  cultured  in  Dulbecco’s  Modified  Eagle’s 
Medium  (DMEM)  containing  10%  FBS  at  37°C  with  5% 
CO2.  The  dual-luciferase  reporter  plasmids  were  con-
structed  by  inserting  the  wild-type  (WT)  or  mutant 
(MUT)  3’-untranslated  region  (3’UTR)  of  FSCN1  into 
the GP-miRGLO vector. The WT plasmid contained the 
putative  miR-145  binding  sites,  while  the  MUT  plas-
mid  carried  site-directed  mutations  in  the  seed  regions. 
The  experiments  were  conducted  in  four  groups,  each 
with  three  replicates  (n = 3).  The  groups  were  FSCN1-
WT  plasmid + miR-145  mimics  negative  control  (NC), 
FSCN1-WT  plasmid + miR-145  mimics,  FSCN1-MUT 
plasmid + miR-145  mimics  NC,  and  FSCN1-MUT  plas-
mid + miR-145  mimics.  Plasmids  were  transfected  into 
the  corresponding  cells.  Following  transfection,  100  µL 
of  1  ×  passive  lysis  buffer  (PLB)  was  added  to  the  cells. 
After thorough lysis, the cell suspension was transferred 
to Eppendorf (EP) tubes and placed under a biochemical 
luminescence detector (Turner Biosystems, USA), where 
the  first  reading  was  recorded.  To  each  tube,  50  µL  of 
reaction  termination  solution  was  added,  gently  mixed, 
and then retested, recording the fluorescence signal ratio, 
followed by statistical analysis.

Cell counting kit-8 (CCK-8) for viability tests

Cells  from  each  treatment  group  were  seeded  into 
96-well  plates,  with  2 × 103  cells  per  well.  Each  group 
had  6  replicates,  and  the  plates  were  then  incubated  in 
a  cell  incubator  for  24–96  h.  Every  24  h,  one  plate  was 
taken out. The original culture medium was carefully dis-
carded, and the plate was washed with fresh PBS. Subse-
quently, 100 µL of fresh culture medium containing 10% 
CCK-8 detection reagent was added to each well, and the 
plate was incubated in the dark for 2 h in the incubator. 

The absorbance of each well was then measured using a 
microplate reader at the wavelength of 450 nm.

Cell migration assay

Cells  were  resuspended  in  serum-free  medium,  adjust-
ing  the  cell  concentration  to  2.0 × 105  cells/mL.  Then, 
200  µL  of  cell  suspension  was  added  to  the  upper  layer 
of the chamber (sterile transwell with 8.0 μm pore poly-
carbonate  membrane  insert,  purchased  from  Corning, 
USA),  while  600  µL  of  cell  culture  medium  containing 
10% FBS was added to the lower layer. The culture plate 
was  then  placed  in  the  incubator  for  16  h.  After  PBS 
washing,  the  chamber  was  fixed  with  4%  paraformalde-
hyde  for  20  min,  followed  by  staining  with  0.5%  crystal 
violet for 10–15 min. Unmigrated cells in the upper layer 
were carefully removed with cotton swabs, and the num-
ber of migrated cells was observed and counted under a 
microscope.

Cell invasion assay

The  matrix  gel  was  pre-melted  on  ice  and  diluted  with 
serum-free medium at a ratio of 1:4. Then, 50 µL per well 
was  added  to  the  upper  layer  of  the  chamber  at  37  °C 
for 30 min to solidify the gel for later use. The cells were 
resuspended  in  serum-free  culture  medium,  where  the 
cell  concentration  was  adjusted  to  2.0 × 105  cells/mL. 
Then, 200 µL of cell suspension was added to the upper 
layer of the chamber, while 600 µL of cell culture medium 
containing  10%  FBS  was  added  to  the  lower  layer.  The 
culture  plate  was  then  placed  in  the  cell  incubator  for 
24  h.  After  PBS  wash,  the  chamber  was  fixed  with  4% 
paraformaldehyde  for  20  min,  followed  by  staining  with 
0.5%  crystal  violet  for  10–15  min.  Non-invasion  cells 
in  the  upper  layer  were  carefully  removed  with  cotton 
swabs,  and  the  number  of  invading  cells  was  observed 
and counted under a microscope.

Cell colony formation assay

Cells  were  seeded  into  3.5  cm  cell  culture  dishes  with 
1 × 103  cells  per  dish  and  then  cultured  in  a  cell  incu-
bator.  The  growth  status  and  density  of  the  cells  were 
monitored  under  a  microscope  on  a  daily  basis.  When 
significant  cell  colony  formation  was  observed,  cell  cul-
ture was immediately halted. After washing with PBS, 4% 
paraformaldehyde  was  used  for  fixation  for  20  min,  fol-
lowed by 0.5% crystal violet staining for 10–15 min. The 
staining  solution  was  then  discarded,  and  the  unbound 
staining  solution  was  rinsed  away  using  PBS.  The  cells 
were  left  to  air  dry  at  room  temperature.  The  size  and 
number of cell colonies were recorded. A cell count > 50 
was considered a positive colony, and the number of cell 
colonies in each group was calculated.

to assess the biodistribution profiles. In a separate experi-
ment, a total of 15 mice were randomly divided into three 
groups  (n = 5  for  each  group),  and  ErNPs,  ErNPs-sEVs 
and ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs were injected into mice via the 
tail vein, at 3-day intervals, for a total of four injections. 
Fluorescence accumulation at the tumor sites was moni-
tored at 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 and 24 h post each injection, along 
with records of the body weights and tumor sizes. In par-
allel, a total of 20 mice were randomly divided into four 
groups (n = 5 for each group), and PBS, miRNA, sEVs and 
miRNA@sEVs were individually injected into each group 
of  mice  via  the  tail  vein,  every  three  days  for  a  total  of 
four injections. The weights of the mice and the sizes of 
their  tumors  were  measured  after  each  injection.  After 
mice  were  euthanized,  the  blood  was  quickly  collected 
for  the  assessment  of  liver  and  kidney  function  param-
eters, specifically aspartate aminotransferase (AST), ala-
nine aminotransferase (ALT), blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 
and  creatinine  (CREA).  Simultaneously,  major  organs 
and  tumors  were  processed  and  sliced  for  pathological 
analysis.

Statistical analysis

All  data  presented  in  this  article  were  presented  as 
mean ± standard  deviation  (SD).  Statistical  comparisons

Preparation and characterization of miRNA-encapsulated 
sEVs (miRNA@sEVs)

Freshly  extracted  sEVs  and  miRNA  mimics  were  thor-
oughly  mixed  in  a  centrifuge  tube,  resulting  in  a  final 
concentration  of  1 × 1010/mL  sEVs  and  100  nM  miRNA 
mimics. The centrifuge tube was placed in the ice water, 
and  the  tip  sonication  parameters  were  set  as  500  V, 
2 kHz, 20% amplitude, 6 cycles, with 5 s pulse/3 s pause 
(QSonicator  500,  SONICS,  USA).  This  process  was 
repeated twice with a 2-min interval on ice to cool down. 
Next,  the  solution  was  transferred  to  an  electrode  cup, 
and the electroporation conditions were set to 110 V and 
940  µF,  using  the  CUY21EDIT  II  electroporator  (BEX, 
Japan).  After  electroporation,  the  mixture  was  centri-
fuged  at  100,000  g  for  2  h  to  remove  unbound  miRNA, 
resulting in the precipitation of miRNA@sEVs.

Fluorescent labeling of miRNA@sEVs

6.4  mg/mL  sEVs  and  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  incubated 
in  the  dark  at  37  °C  for  30  min.  ErNPs  were  purchased 
from  Nirmidas  Biotech,  USA,  and  well  characterized 
as  reported  [21].  Basically,  they  were  synthesized  as 
α-phase  Er-doped  NaYF4  nanocrystal  and  functional-
ized  with  PEG-NH2  group  to  give  off  enhanced  bright 
downconversion fluorescence upon excitation at 980 nm 
(size = ~ 14 nm; λex/λem=980 nm/1540 nm). Subsequently, 
the  mixture  was  placed  in  an  ultrasonic  water  bath  and 
sonicated  for  3  min.  Then,  the  liquid  was  transferred  to 
100  kDa  MWCO  ultrafiltration  tubes  and  centrifuged 
at  1,500  g  for  30  min  at  4  °C  to  remove  unbound  dyes. 
We also investigated the possible dye leakage in the fresh 
cell-free  media  over  time  after  sEVs  were  stained  by 
ErNPs. Specifically, the fluorescence of the newly stained 
miRNA@sEVs  was  recorded  as  the  initial  fluorescence 
intensity and kept incubated at 37 °C up to 24 h. The sam-
ples  were  taken  at  different  time  points  and  transferred 
to  the  ultrafiltration  tube  and  centrifuged  at  1500  ×  g 
for  30  min  to  separate  the  dye  stained  sEVs  and  super-
natant. The fluorescence of supernatant was measured by 
the DeepVision NIR-II in vivo imaging system (Nirmidas 
Biotech, USA). The fluorescence intensity of the obtained 
supernatant  at  each  time  point  was  normalized  to  the 
initial  fluorescence  intensity,  obtaining  the  cumulative 
release of dyes from stained sEVs as a function of time.

poration followed by sonication, and sonication followed 
by  electroporation,  respectively.  The  qRT-PCR  was  uti-

expression  in  each  group  was  measured  and  compared. 
Compared  to  the  direct  incubation,  the  electropora-

the  sonication  had  a  2.2-fold  increase,  the  electropora-
tion plus sonication achieved a 5.6-fold increase, and the 
sonication  followed  by  electroporation  attained  a  5.9-

troporation (Fig. 3A).

In vivo profiles of miRNA@sEVs

We  investigated  in  vivo  profiles  of  miRNA@sEVs  in 
murine cancer models. NIR-II fluorescent probes ErNPs 
were  adopted  to  stain  sEVs  or  miRNA@sEVs,  and  their 
fluorescent  properties  were  measured  to  determine  the 
dye  concentration  and  physical  stability  (Supplementary 
File  1:  Figure  S6A).  Firstly,  the  fluorescent  linear  range 
of  ErNPs  was  examined.  The  original  solution  of  ErNPs 
was diluted at ratios of 1:1, 1:2, 1:5, 1:10, 1:20, 1:50, 1:100, 
1:200,  and  1:500  in  PBS.  The  NIR-II  small  animal  live 
imaging instrument was applied to measure the fluores-
cence intensity versus each concentration at λex/λem=980 
nm/1540  nm.  The  results  showed  that  the  fluorescence 
intensity of ErNPs increased linearly when the concentra-
tion  fell  in  the  range  of  0–1  mg/mL.  Thus,  1  mg/mL  of 
ErNPs was determined for the working concentration in 
the following experiments.

Subsequently,  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  incubated  with 
sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs,  respectively,  and  the  labeled 
particles were transferred to ultracentrifugation tubes at 
different time points (i.e., 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, and 24 h after 
labeling), followed by thorough PBS washing and fluores-
cence determination of ErNPs-labeled sEVs or miRNA@
sEVs. The fluorescence intensity of the obtained superna-
tant at each time point was normalized to the initial fluo-
rescence  intensity  of  ErNPs-stained  sEVs  or  miRNA@
sEVs,  and  the  cumulative  release  of  ErNPs  from  stained 
particles  was  obtained  over  time.  The  results  demon-
strated  that  the  initial  release  of  ErNPs  from  stained 
sEVs or miRNA@sEVs showed a linearly increasing trend 
over time but finally reached a plateau after 15 h release 
(Supplementary File 1: Figure S6B). Thereby, for later ani-
mal  experiments,  1  mg/mL  ErNPs  were  first  incubated 
with  sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs,  respectively,  for  > 15  h  to 
ensure the staining stability (i.e., no further dye leakage). 
Afterwards, ErNPs-sEVs and ErNPs-miRNA@sEVs were 
prepared  and  injected  into  mice  bearing  HCT116  sub-

tion, the dimension of tumors reached 0.8–0.9 cm in all 
groups.

The in vivo images of mice at various time points were 
illustrated  in  Fig.  4A.  Concurrently,  venous  blood  was 
collected  from  mice  to  assess  the  pharmacokinetics  of 
sEVs  and  miRNA@sEVs  (Fig.  4B),  while  the  accumula-

Discussion
In this study we first verified that miR-145 was an effec-
tive  tumor  suppressor  in  clinical  samples  from  patients 
with  CRCs,  and  it  exerted  its  tumor-inhibitory  effect  by 
downregulating its primary target FSCN1. Then, we uti-
lized sEVs derived from hucMSCs as delivering carriers to 
encapsulate miR-145 and enhanced the loading efficiency 
of miR-145 in sEVs by employing a strategic combination 

of sonication and electroporation techniques. The result-
ing  miRNA@sEVs  demonstrated  exceptional  biocom-

in  the  bloodstream  and  increased  accumulation  within 
tumors.  Consequently,  these  nanoscaled  miRNA@sEVs 
showed  substantial  suppression  of  tumor  progression 
both  in  vitro  and  in  vivo  by  effectively  downregulating 
the expression of FSCN1 protein.

Recent research suggests that miR-145 is implicated in 
various  malignant  tumors  by  regulating  oncogenes  and 
signal  transduction  related  to  cell  proliferation,  angio-
genesis,  tumor  progression,  metastasis,  and  therapeutic 
resistance  [22].  For  instance,  miR-145  has  been  identi-
fied as a diagnostic marker for chondrosarcoma, where it 
may inhibit the tumor progression by downregulating the 
expression of FSCN1 [23]. Similarly, miR-145 was found 
to be downregulated in hepatocellular carcinoma, reduc-
ing cancer cell proliferation by targeting insulin receptor 
substrate  1  [24].  Moreover,  miR-145  can  suppress  non-
small cell lung cancer by downregulating its dual targets, 
GOLM1 and RTKN [25].

One  miRNA  may  target  multiple  gene  transcripts 
within one specific cancer type, and the primary targets 
can vary in different stages of the same cancer or across 
different  types  of  cancers  [26].  In  human  CRCs,  miR-
145 may modulate a pool of gene targets at each step of

have  been  reported.  MiR-145  may  bind  directly  to  and

is needed to clarify whether and how miR-145 can bind 
its various gene targets and regulate tumor development 
during different stages of CRC.

Here we delineated that miR-145 deliverd by hucMSC-
derived  sEVs  primarily  targeted  FSCN1  and  effectively 
lowered  its  expression  in  CRCs,  thereby  inhibiting  cell 
proliferation,  colony  formation,  migration  and  invasion, 
which  eventually  led  to  substantial  tumor  suppression. 
Notably,  the  interaction  between  miR-145  and  FSCN1 
has  been  reported  in  several  malignant  tumors,  where 
FSCN1 expression was negatively correlated to miR-145 
[32, 33]. Specifically downregulated by certain long non-
coding RNA inhibition [34] or by promoter hypermethyl-
ation [35], the loss of miR-145 expression, which directly 
interacts  with  3’-untranslated  region  of  FSCN1  messen-
ger  RNA,  upregulates  FSCN1  expression  at  the  mRNA 
and posttranscriptional levels, so promoting tumor pro-
gression  [36,  37].  Our  results  here  validated  the  role  of 
miR-145/FSCN1  axis  in  CRC  progression,  which  stood 
well in line with those reports.

Highly  conserved  across  species,  human  FSCN1  pro-
tein  is  widely  expressed  in  various  organs,  which  cross-
links  actin  microfilaments  into  well-structured  bundles, 
providing rigidity and stability for cytoskeleton remodel-
ing and cell adhesion/migration [38]. Aberrantly elevated 
levels  of  FSCN1  have  been  found  in  a  variety  of  cancer 
types,  closely  associated  with  promoted  cell  prefiltra-
tion,  migration  and  invasion,  and  neovascularization, 
thus being recognized as a poor prognostic indicator and 
a  potential  druggable  target  [39–41].  In  prostate  cancer 
high expression of FSCN1 induces cytoskeleton reorgani-
zation, aggregating actin bundles into filamentous pseu-
dopodia,  therefore  promoting  migration,  invasion  and 
lymph  node  metastasis  [42].  Alternatively,  FSCN1  con-
tributes  to  lung  adenocarcinoma  development  through 
activation  of  PI3K/AKT  signaling  pathway,  stimulat-
ing  cell  proliferation  and  inhibiting  cell  apoptosis  [43]. 
In  hepatoblastoma,  FSCN1  activates  the  Wnt/β-catenin 
pathway  by  stabilizing  the  entry  of  β-catenin  into  the 
nucleus  and  driving  the  transcription  of  oncogenes 
[44].  Nevertheless,  with  regards  to  the  ensuing  FSCN1-
mediated  tumor  progression  in  CRC,  it  requires  further 
investigation to explore the exact mechanism or pathway 
following miR-145 regulation.

Derived  from  their  parental  cells,  sEVs  possess  high 
biocompatibility  and  low  immunogenicity  due  to  their 
endogenous  origin.  Their  surface  proteins  help  evade 
immune  detection,  reducing  clearance  by  the  mononu-
clear  phagocyte  system.  HucMSC-derived  sEVs  inherit 
the  homing  characteristics  of  parental  cells  and  can 
actively recognize the tumor microenvironment through 
adhesion  molecules  such  as  integrins  [45].  In  contrast, 
artificial  particles  at  similar  nano  to  micro  scale,  lipo-
somes  for  example,  albeit  surface  modification  such  as 
tunable PEGylation may reduce immune recognition, can 
still  provoke  an  array  of  immune  responses  and  induce 
local  or  systemic  toxicity  [46].  At  the  same  time,  the 
targeting  capacity  of  liposomes  relies  on  the  enhanced 
permeability  and  retention  (EPR)  effect,  whereas  tumor 
vascular  heterogeneity  may  greatly  limit  their  efficien-
cies [47]. Furthermore, cell-derived sEVs and synthesized 
liposomes can both efficiently carry xenobiotic drugs for 
delivery,  while  sEVs  own  unique  therapeutic  pleiotropy 
as it can  inherit biologically active molecules  from their 
parental cells. For this reason, with similar efforts to load 
exogenous  cargos  of  pharmaceutical  interest  into  both 
drug  carriers,  endogenous  substances  in  sEVs  can  be 
exploited  to  take  synergistic  effects  for  enhanced  treat-
ment [48].

Efficiently  loading  therapeutic  substances  (such  as 
chemical  drugs  and  exogenous  nucleic  acids)  into  sEVs 
and precisely delivering them to the specific target in the 
body may govern the effectiveness of cancer therapy. To 
begin, gene cargos can be encapsulated into sEVs through 

direct  or  indirect  method.  The  direct  method  employs 
physical or/and chemical techniques to import the cargo 
directly  into  sEVs,  including  incubation,  electropora-
tion,  sonication,  extrusion  and  freeze-thaw  cycles.  In 
contrast,  the  indirect  loading  first  integrates  the  gene 
into  the  donor  cells  through  gene  transfection  and  co-
incubation,  followed  by  the  secretion  and  isolation  of 
sEVs  [49].  In  this  study  we  selected  sEVs  derived  from 
hucMSCs  as  the  delivery  platform  to  encapsulate  miR-
145 via a combination of sonication and electroporation. 
Compared  to  direct  incubation  with  very  low  efficiency, 
this combinational method achieved a 5.9-fold improve-
ment of miRNA loading, much higher than electropora-
tion  or  sonication  alone.  This  loading  capacity  was  also 
superior to our previous result when miR-193 was loaded 
into hucMSC-derived sEVs via sonication with optimized 
energy input [18]. Simultaneously, encapsulation of miR-
NAs by sEVs protected them from immature degradation 
before reaching the target, exerting tumor suppression to 
the best of their capacities [18]. Put together, sEVs prove 
themselves as exceptional gene drug delivery vehicles in 
cancer therapy.

To  date,  NIR-II  fluorescence  bioimaging  has  found 
widespread  applications  in  the  biomedical  field,  with 
single-walled  carbon  nanotubes,  quantum  dots,  gold 
nanoparticles,  and  rare  earth  nanoparticles  commonly 
implemented as contrast agents. Compared to NIR-I, the 
NIR-II  fluorescence  imaging  window  offers  higher  spa-
tial resolution and allows deeper tissue penetration [50]. 
To monitor and track the circulation of miRNA@sEVs in 
vivo in a real-time manner, we utilized ErNPs as a tracer 
probe, examining the pharmacokinetics and tumor accu-
mulation  of  miRNA@sEVs.  Our  results  indicated  that 
miR-145 encapsulation had no noticeable impact on the 
pharmacokinetics  of  husMSC-derived  sEVs,  displaying 
a  circulation  half-life  of  approximately  4  h,  consistent 
with  our  previous  findings  [47].  Similarly,  the  presence 
or  absence  of  miR-145  did  not  significantly  alter  the 
accumulation  of  sEVs  at  tumor  sites,  showing  an  initial 
increase  followed  by  a  gradual  decline  until  clearance 
from the body, aligning with our earlier reports [18, 47]. 
Importantly, miR-145 loaded and delivered by sEVs suc-
cessfully  inhibited  tumor  progression  by  downregulat-
ing FSCN1 expression in the xenografted murine model 
of  human  CRC.  Those  results  further  demonstrated  the 
excellent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, high sta-
bility,  and  minimized  toxicity  of  sEVs  as  a  delivery  plat-
form  of  bioactive  materials,  such  as  therapeutic  nucleic 
acids.

Conclusion
In  this  study,  we  fabricated  miRNA-encapsulated  sEVs 
using  a  combination  of  sonication  and  electroporation. 
We  employed  ErNPs  as  an  NIR-II  fluorescence  tracer 

Chen et al. Stem Cell Research & Therapy          (2025) 16:343  for  miRNA@sEVs,  allowing  us  to  elucidate  their  bio-
logical  profiles  in  vivo,  including  the  circulation  time, 
biodistribution,  and  tumor  accumulation.  Our  results 
demonstrated  that  miRNA@sEVs,  after  effectively  load-
ing  of  miR-145  into  sEVs,  greatly  inhibited  the  progres-
sion of CRC by downregulating the expression of FSCN1 
as  its  primary  target.  This  study  offers  a  new  strategy 
that  utilizes  sEVs  as  a  biosafe  and  reliable  delivery  plat-
form, enabling non-invasive real-time monitoring of gene 
therapy during tumor treatment under an NIR-II fluores-
cence regimen.
